paras: The rescue of Wayman Sutton was a jail delivery at Wytheville, Wythe County, Virginia, early on November 29, 1888, when a band of armed, masked men broke into the county jail and freed Sutton, who was to be hanged the next day for murder. No one was injured, and Governor Fitzhugh Lee offered rewards and accused local officials of neglect. Papers noted that the conviction rested on circumstantial evidence and that another man claimed the killing; a New York paper wrote that lynch law had "taken a change of character."

Peter Harvell of Wythe County was shot and killed at his door on May 19, 1887, while his wife and mother held him up. Suspicion fell on Sutton and his father-in-law, Morgan Pendleton, who had been seen near the house; Pendleton escaped, and Sutton was arrested outside the state and convicted at the March term. After an appeal failed, Judge Brown fixed the execution for November 30.

Sutton's friends petitioned for clemency, and Lee received a letter signed "M. M. Pendleton, or M. Mitchell," whose writer said he alone had shot Harvell, "inspired by God," and that Sutton was innocent. Lee found no reason to credit it and declined to interfere on November 24.

According to the Alexandria Gazette, it was rumored the evening before that a party was forming near Rural Retreat, and the sheriff summoned a posse to guard the jail. The Richmond Dispatch's Wytheville correspondent wrote that the rescuers arrived on an east-bound train from near Rural Retreat and got off at a cut above town.

At about 3 o'clock the men broke the jail door with a sledge-hammer, filled the hall with double-barreled guns and pistols, and held the jailer at gunpoint. When he refused them the keys, they found them in his wife's sewing machine, took Sutton, locked some guards in a cell, and left for the west end of the county. Sheriff J. R. Harkrader telegraphed the governor that armed men had overpowered the guards and asked, "What should be done?"

Lee offered $1,000 for Sutton's recapture and told Commonwealth's Attorney J. L. Gleaves that, if the rescue had been rumored beforehand, officials had shown "gross neglect of duty." He told the Dispatch that Wythe County had seen "seven murders and two lynchings" without punishment. On November 30 he proclaimed $1,000 for the rescuers, and a San Antonio paper reported that the town added $1,000 for Sutton's capture.

On December 8 Deputy Sheriff John B. Hurt examined a prisoner at Bowling Green suspected of being Sutton and said, "He is not the man I want." Wytheville travelers told the Dispatch that the town had expected the jail delivery and the sheriff had stayed at his house. A reward circular was still circulating in mid-December, and no report of a recapture or of arrests of the rescuers appears in the coverage.

Virginia papers treated the rescue as a defeat for the law rather than a lynching. The Dispatch headlined "Gallows Cheated" and "Daring Act of a Mob" while its correspondent called the rescuers "a party of friends"; the Alexandria Gazette wrote "Rescue of a Murderer" and the Washington Evening Star "The Wytheville Jail Delivery."

Outside the state most papers used a Lynchburg Advance special. The Memphis Appeal ran it as "A Lynching in Virginia" with the deck "A Murderer Strung Up," although its text described a rescue, while the Louisville Courier-Journal spoke of "a Band of Masked Friends" and a New Mexico weekly added "Presumption That He Was Innocent." A separate dispatch in the Rock Island Argus, "The Law Defied Again," was the only one to call Sutton "white."

The New York Evening World wrote that "justice seems to have been the victim" and called the rescue "public sentiment misdirected" and "characteristically American." Into December, roundup columns from Kentucky to Dakota and Connecticut reported the rescue.

Estimates of the party ran from "not more than thirty" (the Dispatch correspondent) to one hundred to two hundred (the sheriff) and "near two hundred" (later informants), with fifty to one hundred in the wire. The wire dated Harvell's murder to March 1887 and Sutton's arrest to Indiana, while the Dispatch placed the arrest in Illinois.

reader.title: Rescue of Wayman Sutton
bases: An armed, masked band broke into the Wytheville jail and freed a condemned prisoner without harming him; no one was killed or attacked as punishment (A6, A7, A22).

A band of at least twenty-five men acted illegally in breaking into the jail, but they freed Sutton rather than killing him, and no one was reported injured (A7, A22). The Memphis Appeal's 'Lynching' and 'Strung Up' headline is contradicted by its own text (A6).
The Dispatch's Wytheville special, the sheriff's telegram, the Lynchburg Advance wire and the Valley Virginian agree that armed men broke the jail and freed Sutton (A6, A7, A11, A22).

framing.detail: Richmond Dispatch: 'Gallows Cheated', 'Daring Act of a Mob', while printing its correspondent's 'party of friends' and the governor's rebuke.
Memphis Appeal ran the Advance special under 'A Lynching in Virginia ... A Murderer Strung Up', contrary to its text.
Courier-Journal and Los Cerrillos Rustler headings stress 'Masked Friends' and a 'Presumption That He Was Innocent'.
New York Evening World: 'justice seems to have been the victim'; 'public sentiment misdirected'; 'characteristically American'.
Valley Virginian and roundup briefs report the rescue and the reward without comment.

conflicts.note: The Dispatch correspondent and a private telegram to the governor gave the lowest figures; the sheriff's higher figure came from the official accused of neglect.
'November 20' contradicts 'the day preceding' the Nov. 30 hanging in the same item (A29) and is a misprint for the 29th.
The victim's name is also printed Harvey, Harwell and Harevill.

Jail break with a sledge-hammer, jailer held at gunpoint, guards locked up, prisoner freed; no hanging (only the Memphis headline says 'Strung Up').
Convicted of the murder of Peter Harvell and sentenced to hang Nov. 30, 1888; appeals and clemency had failed.
Sutton is called 'white' in one Lynchburg dispatch; no other race is given.
Unidentified masked band, called Sutton's 'friends', from near Rural Retreat.
Sutton was taken out and set free; his whereabouts were unknown and rewards were offered for him and his rescuers.
